Jabra Stealth Bluetooth Headset - Black (US Version) I am pleased with this headset; the sound quality is good and audibility is very sharp. The music quality is also good. Assembly is very simple and needs no additional tools to set it together. It also fits well into my ears. I have been using this set for the last three weeks and it works great. It is paired with my cell phone and I use this to listen to the incoming calls and also listen to the music from micro SD card inserted into the cell phone. It is small and has a discreet design. It is very light, easy to carry and works great. The gadget also synchronizes easily with phone, but it does not pair with my Garmin Nuvi GPS machine or my Acer Chromebook both of which are Bluetooth-enabled.

Pairing with cell phone is very easy; just turn the headset on and the cell phone on, it detects the Bluetooth easily and within a minute it gives the message that it is paired. The built-in battery is excellent, and on one charge it lasts for about 5-6 hours of use time. The downside is that this piece doesn't have a separate mute button or the volume button; you have to control volume from your cell phone. Another negative feature is that the three replacement parts for earpiece that comes with the set are of same size, hence gives little option for someone with small (or large) ears. I have rated this product four stars for overall satisfaction.

text_fidelity_a:
THINKWARE TW-X350 Dash Cam with 1080P Sony Exmor Sensor, Wi-Fi, & 2.7" LCD Screen Frustrating. Could not get the iPhone app to work at all, I'd slide the WiFi button to be informed that the WiFi was not functioning. Do I need to set up a local hotspot to use the WiFi feature to download the videos? Which appears to be about the only distinguishing feature of this dashcam. This is NOT a Sony product, apparently it uses licensed Sony technology. The dashcam itself is reasonably well designed. There's a horrid mechanical-female voice which I don't see how to disable. The user experience overall is poor. The manual is not bad as far as legibility, but the content is minimum. Minimal content in four or five languages.

The mounting scheme is atrocious, a joke. I'm not going to put self-adhesive cable anchors anywhere in my car, period. It's just plain dumb. I'm tempted to use a suction cup mount from another dashcam. Or cable ties on my rear-view mirror. But if you're homebrewing a solution right out of the box, maybe you're better off with another product altogether. The mounting suggestion is just a show-stopper. Not a good thing.

The video itself seems good, I mean, dashcams in general are fascinating and useful. But if you're expecting to have consumers put something in their car, it had been not involve defacing any part of the car or reducing its value. Leftover adhesive footprints would be an obvious problem.

I'm uploading a photo of the box. Green type on a black background. Not really a great design. Generally type and packaging tells you more about a product than the manufacturer might have intended. Just not that sophisticated.

Overall there are better dashcams out there. The ability to use WiFi to download video from the camera seemed promising, but I couldn't get it to work at all. The audio feedback from the device was far too loud and I couldn't turn it off. The mounting idea was dead on arrival, not happening.

Disappointing. Cannot recommend this product. A swing and a miss, as they say in baseball.
text_fidelity_b: THINKWARE TW-X350 Dash Cam with 1080P Sony Exmor Sensor, Wi-Fi, & 2.7" LCD Screen

text_fidelity_a:
Sony Digital Flash Voice Recorder (ICD-PX312) This was bought to replace a tape unit to record class lectures for about $50. It is was a major upgrade. It's compact. When you can make recordings they come with a date and time in the file info which makes sorting them much easier. You can also record in to different folders, though you can only edit the folder names on a computer. I have also used this with an external microphone, with which it also worked well.

I use this recorder with NIMH batteries, but it doesn't seem to like them given how it stops recording when the charge of the batteries drops to 40% (tested separately afterwards). I guess this is really meant to be used with alkaline batteries. When the unit quit in class, which I could tell because it beeps when it turns off, I reached for my cell phone. Listening to the cell phone recording afterwards and comparing it to this device I can tell that the cell phone records with background noise and at low sensitivity. While I like that I can use my cell phone as a backup, it would not be my first choice for recording lectures. The recordings from this device, in contrast, have little noise and sound clear.

text_fidelity_a:
ClearStream Micron-R Indoor HDTV Antenna with Reflector - 35 Mile Range I have a roof-top antenna that worked well for analog stations but, when I converted to digital, I went from receiving 8 stations to just 1. After trying a few other antennas, I came across the ClearStream 4. I'm able to pull in 20+ digital stations perfectly, and 4 more so-so. Several analog stations come in as well, but the picture is not nearly as good as the digitial stations.

The antenna is well-made, but is a bit of a pain to assemble - lots of pieces to screw together. It only takes about 10 minutes, but you'll probably need to utter a few choice words since it's hard to get the screws to line up properly. The directions are pretty spotty, but give you the essential information. The brackets are heavy-duty, and everything is either aluminum or plastic, so it should hold up well to the elements if I put it outside. Right now, it is in my attic, and may stay there since it pulls in all the stations I want to watch. It does not come with a cable.

It's pretty compact given its performance, and much more compact that the DB8 (another Antenna Direct model with about the same specifications). Very happy with the performance. Also have a DB2 -- see my comments on that review that compare it to this antenna in terms of performance.
text_fidelity_b: ClearStream Micron-R Indoor HDTV Antenna with Reflector - 35 Mile Range

The price difference between these 2 models is relatively small, but I think additional features on the A2's is more than worth the price. The A1's might be a little over-priced at $60, while the A2's are a bargain at $80.

The A2's have noise cancellation, many more equalization settings that are easy to set via the smartphone app, upgradable firmware, and larger speaker drivers. The Soundcore smartphone app does not work with the A1's. All the extra features give the A2 earbuds noticeably better sound quality while also being easier to use. The A1's have decent sound quality, but there are a lot of $50 wireless earbuds that are just as good. On the other hand, the A2's feature and sound combination is better than any other $80 wireless earbuds that I have tried.

Nikon AF-S Nikkor 50mm f/1.8G Lens I am a professional photographer. I usually shoot Pentax. I bought a Nikon DSLR as a backup to my Pentax K-1 Mark II. This camera would be used if my professional gear should need repair.

I bought the Nikon D5600 with the 18-55 f/3.5 to 5.6 VR lens. I added a 55-300 AF-S VR lens and this AF-S 50mm f/1.8 lens. This lens is just as sharp as the Pentax SMC 50mm f/1.8 lens my wife uses on her Pentax KP.

I'll be using this lens and the D5600 as a portrait backup for my Pentax K-1-II and the AF-D* 50mm f/1.4 AW lens. At the price of this Nikon "nifty fifty" it's a great investment.

When I have the need, I am not afraid to spend a lot of money on equipment; nevertheless, it is nice to know that I can buy a great lens without having to spend a thousand dollars or more. text_fidelity_a:
G.G.Martinsen Black 16 G Mini Usb Port Slim Small Multi-ling I've had the opportunity to review three different G.G. Martinsen players, and of the three this one is my favorite. I brought two of the players, pre-charged, to review at my sister's where I am staying a week while she had and recovers from surgery, and the one thing I can say right off the bat is that I wish the charging cable was of the ubiquitous Micro-A type and not the mini type, which I did not think to bring with me. The [[ASIN:B016F4AGLC other player]] handles like the [[ASIN:B0173CW2CQ first one]] I reviewed for G.G. Martinsen, but I will have to wait until I get back home to do anything other than test the recorder and FM radio on this 16GB player because I have no cable to copy music onto the player with!

Anyway, unlike the other two players, the controls on this one make sense and handle more like what I'm used to. The instructions that come with this (that I also left at home!) were well-written in English, unlike so many products coming out of China these days. But I haven't needed the instructions to figure out how to use this player or change the settings. The first thing I did was set the Power Off and Sleep settings to 0 so the player won't shut off unless I flip the manual switch to turn it off. I have been listening to this player while I've been writing reviews, and I have had absolutely no cutouts with the FM radio even though I'm in a condo sandwiched on all sides by other units and this place is bad with reception of cable TV and other radios. I like that the station stays selected even when you power the player off and on again.

The control dial is easy to see, with a top Menu button, left and right arrows, and a pause/play button on the bottom (something the other players did not have). The round button in the middle has a good tactile feel, and even in the dark it's fairly easy to feel where to press for the different functions. I'll have to re-read the instructions to understand fully when to use the center button and how.

The little piece you can thread a lanyard into is plastic, but I don't think it will break easily unless you put a lot of stress on it. The player comes with a pair of original Apple-style earphones, which are great for walking outside where you need to be able to hear sounds around you while listening to music. The headphones are not the best in the world, but they are a nice additional feature and good to have in situations where you wouldn't want pricier headphones to get ruined (the gym, outside should it start raining). Of course, your listening experience will only be as good as the wired headphones you plug into this player. It really is a whole lot of bang for the buck and an attractive little player. I have the turquoise color, and it's really nice.

I put links to the other two players I have reviewed so you can compare them. What I like about this one is it doesn't have that gimmicky bubble-gum type selection screen but, rather, just has a list of the different features and functions. The list is easy to read and looks more businesslike and professional than the more cartoonish screens of the other two players.
text_fidelity_b: G.G.Martinsen Black 16 G Mini Usb Port Slim Small Multi-ling

If you do not have any of these, the wizzard will set one up for you. It also works with services such as Rhapsody and Live365.

Using the Squeezebox software you then identify where you music files are located and where your playlist information is located and then that is done.

You then turn on your radio. It automatically connects to your WIFI connection in your home. Using either the control knob on the box or the remote control you can choose your radio services. Within 10 minutes of UPS delivering the box I was listening to Sirius, Pandora, and my iTunes music from my upstairs bedroom.

The sound is great. Truly exceptional with full deep bass and clear crisp tenor and high ranges. Even at low volumes the unit sounds great.

The unit also has a sleep timer, clock, and alarm features. There are several presets to set so you can choose favorite songs or stations quickly and easily.

Pros: Easy setup, works with mac or pc. Uses existing services you probably already have. Wonderful sound, small design.

Cons: The only real con I see is that the unit is a little pricy. Also the menus on the unit take a little getting used to as there are many menus and options nested within each other.

Overall this is truly a wonderful product. Great sound, easy setup, and ease of use. Truly great for audiophiles.

Headphone Adapter Converter Supports Audio and Charging for Motorola MotoZ, Letv ,2 in 1 USB-C to 3.5mm Audio Adapter, Nylon Braided 2 in 1 USB Type C Cable Fast Charge to 3.5mm Audio Jack(Black) This is a much easier alternative to the My K-cup option if you want to use your own coffee in a K-cup machine rather than the pre-packaged cups. Unlike the My K-cup you don't need to remove the inner cup of the machine to use this. It just drops right in, so you can switch between this and a regular k-cup without having to dismantle anything.

The kit is very complete. There are three cups, each a slightly different color (different shades of brown). The cups are decently made. The plastic sides are nice and thick; the o-ring on the cap is of good quality; and the metal mesh is firmly attached. My only quibble with the build quality is the hinge. It's plastic, and I don't have confidence that it will last a long time before breaking. It's not a big deal, since the cup will still work fine even with a broken hinge, so I'm not docking any points due to that potential problem.

I like that the water dispersion channel has slots all around it to ensure water gets sprayed in all directions inside the cup to keep the grounds uniformly wet. I also really like that the lip area has a slight indent to make it very easy to pop open the top with one hand.

It fit fine in my Cuisinart K-cup machine. The lid of the machine was just slightly raised compared with using a "real" k-cup, but it had zero impact on performance. I tried several different brews, all with good results. You will need to fiddle with the grind level to get the best coffee. Too fine of a grind and it gets over-extracted and bitter; too coarse and it's weak.

Cleaning a used cup is very easy. I pop open the top, hold it upside down in the compost pail, and whack it gently on the base with a wooden spoon. Nearly all the used grounds drop out, and what's left can be easily rinsed under running water. You can also just dump the contents into the disposal or garbage if you don't compost your grounds.

Another option is to use a mini filter in the cup. A package of them are included and, while they do make cleanup easier, I prefer to use just the cup without a filter.

The kit also includes a charcoal filter. I didn't use that, so I can't speak to its performance. It looks to be the same size as the filters used in the water intake of my Cuisinart K-cup machine, so I expect it would perform in a similar fashion.

This Smart Cup kit works well, is well-made/designed, and comes in a very complete kit. Having used the My K-cup version I can confidently say that this performs better and is easier to use. Highly recommend.

text_fidelity_a:
Pioneer SP-BS22-LR Andrew Jones Home Audio Bookshelf Loudspeakers (Set of 2) If you're like me, you've done some research (extensively in my case) on comparing these two speakers, and have probably come out with a vague case for each of them. Some prefer the Miccas, some prefer the Pioneers. I decided to order both and find out what the deal is for myself. And although I haven't ordered many speakers, I've been a headphone enthusiast for many years.

FYI, I'm using these with a sub (Dayton 1200), so I can't comment on their performance by themselves.

The Miccas sound pretty good, with clear highs - solid performers for movies. But they never made me very impressed by their sound. They seem serviceable, good for the price but not particularly great. They are by no means a bad speaker, but they are a bit thin sounding, kind of one-note.

With the Miccas, if felt like I was listening to music, but with the Pioneers, I felt like I was feeling it. They have a lush tone that is very musical, and I noticed I was bobbing my head to some songs I wasn't before. Better dynamics, soundstage - they really allow you to get lost in the music. Even though the driver size is the same, everything sounds bigger, with more depth.

And even though they have less treble energy than the MB42X, they seem to retrieve a bit more detail. Certainly not "veiled", just darker in tone. I'd prefer there to be slightly less treble than too much - just make sure to remove the grill, as it can make them slightly too dark.

For $20 extra bucks currently I think it's a no-brainer to get the Pioneers, unless you can't particularly stand speakers on the warmer side. I have the center channel coming in today - I've heard mixed reports on it, but if it's anything like the bookshelves I'm sure I'll be satisfied.
text_fidelity_b: Pioneer SP-BS22-LR Andrew Jones Home Audio Bookshelf Loudspeakers (Set of 2)

USB Power Strip Portable Travel Charger Outlets 2.1AMP 1AMP 21W 5Foot Power Supply Cord With Universal Plug Input From 100v-240v Power Sockets USB Charger Station 4 Port 5v 1A/2.1A USB Charger (White) This is a very unique and awesome product. It wasn't listed near the beginning of my Amazon search results, so it took me a while to find it. But it's AWESOME!!!

The first thing I do when I get to a hotel room or a cruise ship cabin is to set up my charging station. We have phones, iWatches, Kindle, iPad, and rechargable power packs, so we end up having a lot of potential things to charge. Setting up the charging area is a high priority. The best place is on a table or desk, so we can spread out our rat's nest of cables and devices with easy access. However, power outlets are often in inconvenient places, especially on a cruise ship. (On cruises, in the past I would actually bring a small extension cord.)

Anyway, this super clever travel charger solves the problem. I can plug it into the wall outlet, and run the cord up onto a table or desk. It's perfect.

Actually, the 4 USB ports isn't nearly enough for us, so one of these chargers wasn't going to entirely solve my problem. Theoretically, I could use two of them, but that's overkill in the sense that I don't need long two cords. Since this charger has a wall-plug type of outlet on the charger itself, I already have regular wall power at the charger on the table. I don't need to run a second cord from a wall outlet. Therefore, I use a small 4-port USB charger without the cord, and plug that into this charger. That gives me 8 USB ports up on the table for easy access. Here's the 4-port charger without a cord that I plug into this one:
https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B07JH9R89T/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_asin_title_o01_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1

I have never seen a charger with a cord like this before, and I am very impressed with how clever and useful the design is! The one problem I found was with the child protection piece inside the slots on the charger's power socket. (This is the 110V power socket on the charger.) Because of the child protection piece, it can sometimes be very hard to get something plugged into that socket. The protection piece needs to slide to the side, so you can't just push the plug straight in, like you would at a wall socket. You need to put the prongs into the slots at an angle, and pry the protection piece out of the way. It's a pain. So, if you don't need the child protection, and you intend to use that socket, you'll probably want to remove the protection piece.

Here's how to do that. The top surface is a snap-off cover. Pull it up in the middle of one of the side, and slip a little screwdriver in there to carefully pry around and pop it off. Then there's a second cover inside that isn't attached, and will almost just fall out. On the back of that second cover, you'll see the two little springs and the plastic protection piece. Pull out the springs and the protection piece, and then put it all back together.

[NOTE: Do not remove the child protection if there will be children near it, or if you have any other safety concerns about its removal. Remove it at your own discretion and your own risk. I'm not telling you to remove it. I'm just telling you how to remove it if you want to.]

Anyway, I actually went a step further. The socket seems to be designed to accept any plug in the universe, so there are a lot of extra holes and spaces (i.e. it's not just two little slits for the normal US plug). I took white electrical tape, and taped over all the extra holes and spaces on the secondary (internal) cover, leaving just the two slits open. Then after popping on the outer cover, you just see the two open slits. All the other openings are covered internally with the white electrical tape. I think it looks much better, but this is purely a cosmetic step.

At first, it seemed like the clip for the plug is on the wrong side. It's on the same side as the USB ports. If you leave the plug in the clip (and leave the cord wrapped around the charger), then rotate the plug down 90 degrees, you can plug it into a wall outlet and the charger would be flush against the wall, hanging down from the wall socket. That seemed like it should be a nice neat way of using it without extending the cord, if desired. However, you can't do that because the USB ports end up against the wall, and you can't access them. If the clip was on the opposite side, it would work fine. As it currently is, in order to use it, you need to flip it around so the USB ports are facing out. But since the plug clip is on the wrong side, the charger sticks out from the wall at an angle. At first this seemed like a design flaw. Then I read in the instructions where it specifically says you shouldn't do any charging while the cord is wrapped around it. Presumably that's a heat issue. Therefore, it is probably designed this way on purpose, to discourage you from attempting to use the charger with the cord wrapped around it.

The bottom line is that there is no design flaw. It's prefect just the way it is. And you need to unwrap the cord when you use it, which is fine with me, since having the cord extended is the best feature of this charger.

Anyway, I think this is an awesome little gadget.

text_fidelity_a:
Jabra Evolve 65t True Wireless Bluetooth Earbuds, UC Optimized – Superior Call Quality and Connectivity – Passive Noise Cancelling Earbuds with up to 15 hours of Battery Life with Charging Case When reviewing headsets, I don't just pop them on and hit play on a favorite song or take a call. I actually run them through a battery of sound tests from an audio site. I run all sets through the same test to make it fair. First on my PC and then on my iPhone XS. I find it's the best way to make an unbiased review.
• Bass: Poor with a limited range. It also wasn’t balanced between the earbuds.
• High freq: Better than the bass, but still a limited range. It was balanced between the earbuds much better though.
• Rattle: None, but it would be weird if earbuds rattled. Ok that’s not true, I stepped on a pair at the gym that rattled afterwards. Oops.
• Volume: Sufficient. I don’t blast my earbuds, because I like to keep my hearing. I could turn it low enough to not hear, and loud enough to be uncomfortable.
• Clarity: Isolated for the sound test they did fine. However, outside the site the clarity started to degrade, and on a call was bad enough to be an issue.

The sound check results were mediocre. Bass was lacking, as was the general range of the set. These actually did worse than their cheaper behind the neck set (Jabra Evolve 65e UC).

As for things other than sound, like usability I like to ask myself what I’m looking for and if product meets those expectations. So, here goes:

Would these last the entire workday?
Yes and No, if you take them off to charge during lunch then you will probably be fine. Otherwise no they are going to die out about 75% through a standard 8 hr workday. They require a USB port and their little case thing to charge. I had no issues as long as I remember to charge them at lunch.

Are they easy to use?
The basics, yes. All the extra features, not so much. I opened the box up and was happy to see the quick-start guide, unfortunately if there is a manual I didn't get one. I found a digital copy tucked away in the iPhone app, but nothing in the box itself. That made anything past the basics in the quick-start guide a matter of trial and error, until I found the manual tucked away in the App. For the price, that seems like a rather cheap move. There is a ton of useful info in the manual that is not contained in the quick-start guide.

Can I take calls seamlessly?
Yes, but for me at least the call experience was lacking. The voices on some but not all calls were a bit muddled, however they could hear me just fine. So poor marks for the sound quality, but high marks for the mic.
Speaking of mics, can I mute the mic easily?
Easily, yes. But knowing for sure if you are muted (we've all been there) only when using the computer dongle, on my iPhone using Bluetooth, eek not so much. Had to leave it to faith. That was a bit scary.

Plays music well (aka does it have range and bass)?
Meh. I have the sound review at the top. As you can imagine, lack of bass negatively impacts listening to music. I mean it wasn’t awful but it wasn’t great either.

Can I opt to hear people talking to me (audio pass-through)?
Yes, but it sounds super static and buzzy. The sound is not clear and crisp at all. Also, you can't just pop an earbud out and listen with one ear. If the earbuds are anymore than head-width apart they stop working all together. According to the manual, you should be able to use the right earbud by itself, but that was not my experience. It also would stop working (although it worked a bit longer than the left) once they were too far apart.

Noise-canceling abilities, can I at least block out the cubical next to me?
Sort of. You can block drumming blah blah blah sounds, but ringing phones and coworkers talking, not so much. Although it did take the edge off. The Jabra iPhone app for these has some cool ambient sound machine settings, waves crashing, thunderstorm, white noise, etc. Probably my favorite thing about this whole set.

Are they comfortable?
I didn't like them, but I am a petite human and have small ears. I also don't like the weird vacuuming pressure you feel when wearing anything noise-cancelling. I will give these neutral marks for comfort, I think if you had larger ear canals and didn't mind closed type headsets these would probably be fine.

Are these worth the price?
Nope. For the price these should be spectacular and check all the boxes. They are mediocre in sound quality even though they are packed with features. If you plan on just tossing them on and not actually testing the audio, go for it. They work. But for the price, they should handle music and calls equally well. They do not.

Overall, I will have to say I was rather disappointed with these. I also reviewed their behind the neck version (Jabra Evolve 65e UC) and was hoping I had just gotten a dud with that set. Well lightening either struck twice, or the audio on these is even worse than the cheaper behind the neck version. Darn, because I wanted to love these. I have a soft spot for gadgets with cool features. These had potential. I will give them three stars because if the price point wasn’t so high, they would be okay. Not great, but they’d get the job done. I also really liked the ambient sounds you could listen to on the app. A nice little extra that was unexpected.

Hope that helps!
text_fidelity_b: Jabra Evolve 65t True Wireless Bluetooth Earbuds, UC Optimized – Superior Call Quality and Connectivity – Passive Noise Cancelling Earbuds with up to 15 hours of Battery Life with Charging Case

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Paperwhite, 6" High Resolution Display with Built-in Light, Wi-Fi [Previous Generation] I bought for my mother as a mother's day gift. I also bought a Vera Bradley cover and a $50 Amazon GC to go with it. My mom is not the gadget type. No matter how many times I explain how to change TV setting from the Playstation to the cable box, which for our TV is a one button push, she just cannot do it. So, getting a Kindle was a stretch, however, I wanted her to have the ability to travel without taking a lot of books with her because my mom is also that mom who over packs and has too much stuff, which inevitably means she loses something.

So, the Kindle only gets use when she travel, but she has figured it out somewhat. She can't quite figure out how to purchase books or how to change the settings, which she just gets me to do it for her, but it has gotten a lot of use because she does take it with her instead of a bunch of books. In my use of this Kindle, I find it somewhat clumsy, slow, and some of the icons are not self explanatory and takes a few tries going back and forth. What I do like is that the screen is the exact size of a paperback book, there is no glare whatsoever, which is a problem I have with my iPad, and the light in the screen is perfect for reading at night without a lamp on. The ability to have all of Amazon's e-books at your fingertips is nice if you have a Wi-Fi connection. I don't see a reason to get the 3G as this is just a Kindle for reading only, thus, I and my mother can wait til a Wi-Fi connection is available to download another book if need be. However, you can download multiple books at a time so if you just can't stand not having something to do for 20-30 mins, I would suggest downloading more than one.

Battery life is out of control! I have never seen this go below 50% even after hours of use. One downside is that the plug to charge it is not included so you will have to also pay for that as well. It is also very lightweight, and if you have a little case it's like holding an actual paperback, unlike an iPad which is much heavier and cumbersome to read e-books on.

However, overall, I'm old school. I like paper books. The smell, the ability to write notes and see those notes on the margins, the feel of the paper between my fingers. I can go my references quicker and don't have to worry about running out of memory space because my books stay on a shelf until I need them. So, I recommend this for travel only for the sake making room in your carryon. It is easy to use once you learn all the little quirks. Otherwise, the geek/nerd in me just always goes back to actual black and white.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Paperwhite, 6" High Resolution Display with Built-in Light, Wi-Fi [Previous Generation]

The documentation was not the best, but was sufficient.

text_fidelity_a:
Jabra REVO Corded Stereo Headphones - Retail Packaging - Gray (Discontinued by Manufacturer) When I received the box I was extremely impressed with the sturdieness and attractiveness of the presentation. And although I know that many people don't care about such things, I happen to believe that if such concern is taken with the outside packaging - there is a very good chance the same attention to detail will pertain to the product itself. I was not wrong.

For someone who hasn't had a pair of "real" headphones since the early 80's, I was a little skeptical about the weight on my head, the quality of the sound, and the flexibility of something other than my earbuds. What a wonderful revelation. These headphones are extremely lightweight (in fact I wore them for about 2 hours straight and forgot I had them on when I was getting ready to leave the house), the cord that connects to your device is a very comfortable 48 inches long, they are flexible enough to conveniently fold down and place inside of a small pouch which is included, and as for the sound - it is simply incredible.

The ability to have the Jabra App convert most of my songs into an upgraded Dolby Digital Plus format at no additional cost is the real deal clincher. The music is breathtaking and made me wonder how I ever enjoyed the songs before these came along. Now I carry the little pouch in my purse and take them everywhere.

All I can say in conclusion is that if you really love your music and want to appreciate it at the highest level, for the price these are a wonderful investment. Save the earbuds for the gym, and use these headphones when you truly want to feel the music.
text_fidelity_b: Jabra REVO Corded Stereo Headphones - Retail Packaging - Gray (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

text_fidelity_a:
Wacom Intuos Small Bluetooth Graphics Drawing Tablet, 4 Customizable ExpressKeys, Portable for Teachers, Students and Creators, Compatible with Chromebook Mac OS Android and Windows - Black I love this little tablet. It's an inexpensive way to sketch: Particularly if you get the pistachio, which was $20 less then the boring black one when I bought it. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

I particularly like that it works with Android (at least on phones that support USB OTG, which is most these days). It would have been even better if the Bluetooth worked with Android, but at least with my Pixel 4, it didn't.

It doesn't come with any Android software, but Autodesk Sketchbook is free, and it's quite full of features. Sketchbook also runs on Windows 10.

The pen does not have an eraser like my *really* old Wacom bamboo did (you flipped the pen upside down, and it keyed the erase function). But I got used to it pretty quickly. (On the desktop, you can program one of the buttons on the tablet to switch to eraser). The model with an eraser is a lot more expensive, and I don't know if the eraser would work with Sketchbook in any case.

Corel Painter Essentials seems nice: I haven't used it a lot, because I've usually been on my phone. The first several times, it nagged me to upgrade, but it's stopped doing so. The "AI photo painting" bit is fun, but it's pretty slow, even on a pretty beefy i7. I was hoping that the software had an API, so then I could just auto-generate all of the various options, but it doesn't appear to.

Anyway, it's a ton of fun, and it's got me drawing stuff again.
text_fidelity_b: Wacom Intuos Small Bluetooth Graphics Drawing Tablet, 4 Customizable ExpressKeys, Portable for Teachers, Students and Creators, Compatible with Chromebook Mac OS Android and Windows - Black

text_fidelity_a:
Sony ZX Series Wired On-Ear Headphones with Mic, White MDR-ZX110AP I certainly didn't expect anything of audiophile quality or anything astounding. Knowing how much I'm spending is the context for the review.

It's a good pair of headphones.

They're lightweight, comfortable, the earpads stay reasonably cool, the cord is just long enough to listen to at a desk (and that's a good thing), and they sound awfully good for what I paid. They also look pretty okay. The fact that they fold flat is a nice little bonus but for a pair of utility headphones, I think these are a home run.

So as a sound engineer and a musician I would put it this way. They're not high fidelity headphones, nor do they work for performance. They won't work for reference/studio work at all. They're too flimsy to call a solid pair, but for casually listening to music while multi-tasking at home or for watching a streaming video, these do just great. I think there are a number of good headphones like this one you can get for less than $20 or so. This one is up there and I would buy it again if I needed another.
text_fidelity_b: Sony ZX Series Wired On-Ear Headphones with Mic, White MDR-ZX110AP

text_fidelity_a:
Monster ScreenClean Soft Touch Wipes, Screen Cleaner Wipes for Computer Screens, TV, Phones, Tablets, and Car Touch Screens, Home Office, 70 Count After 40-some years on the technical side of electrochemical fabrication (12" wafer fab) and manufacturing that included the IBM PS1 & PS2 birth … cleanliness is Godliness. I've likely tried every chemical variant of cleaner ever invented, though many fewer are now permitted for USA use.

Though impractical for the laptop, some excellent cleaners in the $1000/gal category might be suggested for cleansing strategic missile-related monitors and surfaces. The value and reliability of what device you are cleaning is the most critical consideration when choosing a cleaner. A wrong choice might pay back immediately with bad results, dissolving the anti-reflective coating or lamination of the touch screen overlay, removing specialized keyboard paints, ruining distinctive finishes, etc. For another, that same choice might do a bang-up job on the big screen at home, but when used on a laptop, it slowly dissolves and/or corrodes critical interconnects as you pass through dewpoints on that 17-hour airplane ride to Sydney.

Q: What is the best cleaner to shine on my $1500 laptop?

A: Not the cheapest $4/qt cleaner. Not one of grandma's window elixirs.

Behind the scenes, there is likely no other technical discussion as critical as cleaning and cleaners. Billions are spent every year on the problem. What I know from experience is that an alcohol solvent-based cleaner does a pretty good job erasing the symbology that makes my lighted keyboard legible. I look for a cleaner to remove the latent crusty-goo residue left by that anti-viral covid computer cleaner six months ago. Some cleaners with notionally benign saponifiers that sell under the enviro-friendly, "Green!", "non-GMO!" moniker is known to corrode solder joints and electro-plating to short the keyboard and LCD/OLED out.

Finding the right balance between solvent and saponifiers has not evolved smoothly. Saponifiers remove organics. The stuff that sprays out of your mouth and nose when yelling at the laptop. Solvents remove inorganics like hand cream, french fry grease, and Cheeto dust. I've rolled up all of this wisdom in my 'Rule #446 - Do not buy the cheapest electronics cleaner. Ever.'

This Monster cleaner is not cheap. It's a premium cleaner under a known premium brand. Given Monster brands, cleaning processes are the #1 priority for their established long-lived high-fidelity interconnection. My laptop has a touch screen that demands a non-delaminating cleaner and a lighted keyboard with that funky paint and laser-etched symbology. This Monster cleaner did an unexpectedly quick, no-smudge job on the laptop. All is good.
text_fidelity_b: Monster ScreenClean Soft Touch Wipes, Screen Cleaner Wipes for Computer Screens, TV, Phones, Tablets, and Car Touch Screens, Home Office, 70 Count

Even at lowest volume it's more than loud enough to be heard. Programming is easy, it charges fast and holds its charge. I get very good reception with it, though I can't speak to what other people might get. That's an individual thing.

text_fidelity_a:
Microsoft Sculpt Ergonomic Wireless Desktop Keyboard and Mouse - Black. Wireless , Comfortable, Ergonomic Keyboard and Mouse Combo with Split Design and Palm Rest. I'm a huge fan of Microsoft keyboards. Never been much of a fan of their office productivity software, but when it comes to keyboards, Microsoft fits my needs to a T. I'm using the Microsoft Digital Media Pro keyboard which (I believe) was discontinued years ago. A shame, since it has so many useful features.

But out with the old and in with the new. I tried and did not care for the previous generation of ergonomic split keyboards from Microsoft. At first glance the Sculpt looked to be a better design. The divide between the two sets of keys did not appear to be as pronounced, and my hands seemed to fit the keyboard very well. Love the feel of the pad on the wrist rest area!

Installation was straightforward, although getting the items out of the box was a challenge. I was happy to see that the necessary batteries were included - nothing worse than having to go hunt for batteries before you can start to use a new device.

The keyboard feel strongly reminded me of a laptop. For some, that may be a good feature. For me it is not. The flat keys and shorter throw makes typing feel "unnatural." I know that sounds vague, but it's the best way I can describe it.

This odd feel translated itself into a much slower typing speed - cut my throughput by about half. Since I write reports for a living, that's a rather big issue.

I also could not come to grips with the function key placement, size and meager supply of ancillary keys. That's a feature I love with my current Media Pro keyboard in that I can map pretty much any of the ample number of multimedia keys to any function I choose, or even a URL. For example, to start SPSS, Excel and WP I press one key. Another single keypress also opens my browser and my Amazon cart URL (and yes, the lettering on that particular key is pretty much worn completely off from use).

Still, if I was forced to, I could live with the keyboard. I could not, under any circumstances, live with the mouse in this set. Feels poor, lacks refinement, and far less versatile than my Logitech M500. I tried my best to get used to the Sculpt mouse, but just grew to hate it the longer I used it.

Now, my opinions are certainly affected by my current choices in keyboards and mice since I've been using them for years and years. I've changed PCs at least three times, but have retained the same keyboard and mouse since they have worked so well. If you have less keyboard/mouse "muscle memory" perhaps the Sculpt will fit the bill. The build quality seems decent, and if they are as reliable as other Microsoft keyboards, it will continue to work for some time. But for me, I just can't move the approval meter past "meh" for the keyboard and "dud" for the mouse. Three stars.
text_fidelity_b: Microsoft Sculpt Ergonomic Wireless Desktop Keyboard and Mouse - Black. Wireless , Comfortable, Ergonomic Keyboard and Mouse Combo with Split Design and Palm Rest.

Panasonic LUMIX DC-ZS70S, 20.3 Megapixel, 4K Digital Camera, Touch Enabled 3-inch 180 Degree Flip-front Display, 30X LEICA DC VARIO-ELMAR Lens, WiFi (Silver) Oct. 2020: If you're photographing foliage with a lot of stems & leaf edges, turn off/down i.Resolution. The "i" isn't that intelligent & makes some nasty over-sharpened halos in some spots. My advice, if you like the overall look of the jpeg, shoot raw+jpeg & process the raw using the jpeg as a guide. This isn't needed all the time. Only some scenes have this problem.
8/14/2020 I never played with the weird 4K burst modes. I just mucked with them today. They tend to hang up the camera. They don't seem to offer much over the regular drive modes. They take up two programmable buttons I can put to better use.
7/18/2019 Low light. No camera of this type is going to do well in natural light at last light (9 PM here.) This one is noticeably worse than my SX720HS. And that's bad.
6/29/2019 With an upgraded SD card, I tried the high speed video. The 240 fps VGA mode worked like a dream. To access it, you have to have the camera on [Cinema Camera]M mode. WARNING: Objects in camera fall 1/8th as fast as real life. :)
6/24/2019. With hundreds of pictures down, I really like the flip screen. I also like the auto bracket. I tend to keep it on 1/3 stop; 2/3 seems to be a bit wide. I've turned off the touch screen. Moving the focus position with the tip of my nose whenever I use the EVF is right out.
6/21/2019. Video playback seems to be twitchy on this model. Apparently some cameras, some times have trouble playing back some videos. Check your memory card specs. Even with a high end card, playback is chancy. Recording is fine. Playback on a PC is fine.

6/17/2019. The only serious negative about this camera is the slight increase in size and weight over my old SX720HS. It's about twice the volume. It has reasons for that, with the added features, particularly the tilt-screen and the EVF.

I really like high-end, 1/2.3"-sensor, long-zoom, point & shoot cameras. This one is pretty close to the limit. Much more and you have to go to 1" sensor designs, which hurts your zoom range. I currently have:
-Canon SX280HS--great camera, still has features no one else has, terrible for videos (I don't care), battery hog (I do care)
-Canon SX720HS--basically the SX280HS perfected. I wouldn't normally upgrade this soon, but for,
-Panasonic ZS70--this camera, which I got for very short money (thanks Amazon warehouse)

* I wasn't that interested in the flip-up screen, I don't do selfies or vlogs. Boy was I wrong. It allows you to snake the camera into positions that would otherwise require a contortionist.
* I was interested in the EVF. It's good in dim light, but I'm used to eyeballing pictures from an external screen. Still a plus, but less of one than I thought.
* I was interested in the powerful bracketing functions. Still interested, but I'll need a bit more study to make it work.

Generally, I shoot in P mode or M mode. Both modes work fine on this camera. The autofocus is better than on the two Canons. The focus modes take a little experimentation to find the one that works best for you, but they all seem to work. 'Standard' color balance is fine. I need to play with 'Natural' a bit to see which one I prefer. The attached photos were all taken on standard. All on a single sunny morning walk after a rainy night in Massachusetts.

First impression? This is a really good camera, even at the list price.
text_fidelity_b: Panasonic LUMIX DC-ZS70S, 20.3 Megapixel, 4K Digital Camera, Touch Enabled 3-inch 180 Degree Flip-front Display, 30X LEICA DC VARIO-ELMAR Lens, WiFi (Silver)

text_fidelity_a:
Archos 9 PC Windows 7 Starter Tablet (Black) Taken for what this is supposed to be, this is a fabulous machine. It's not a primary computer. It's not a laptop replacement. If you need a low power/ultra-portable computer, go with a netbook.

This is more of a mutt. It's a portable media player that doesn't have as much storage as an iPod or a Zen, but has a larger, higher quality screen and a kickstand, which makes it easier to watch movies at a desk.

It can read ebooks. It's not quite as light or comfortable for long term reading as a Kindle, but it can support full color images. It's far superior for this purpose than any of the other devices Amazon has put out an app for.

It can run Windows 7. It's not a full powered machine, but it's even smaller than a netbook.

It fits a slot somewhere between a PDA/smartphone and a netbook, and it's brilliant.

I would have liked a larger hard drive, an SD card (it would have gotten 5 stars if it had one) and more than one USB slot. There is no ethernet port. It only connects wirelessly. The optional port replicator gives you Ethernet and two more USB slots, but still no SD.

A few things to keep in mind. When you're first setting it up, you can't access the virtual keyboard button, so you need to use the Ease of Access icon to get to that. Windows will say to press the space bar to activate the feature. Use the mouse click button (marked +).

The design is very sleek. It's comfortable to hold and work with. The screen has an adjustable brightness, which is easier on the eyes, and easier to use in bright sunlight. The low glare screen helps with this as well.

Overall, this is bleeding edge, early adopter technology.
text_fidelity_b: Archos 9 PC Windows 7 Starter Tablet (Black)

Constructed of water repellant nylon inside and out, this bag is impeccably stitched, has sturdy zippers that work flawlessly, a comfortable carry handle, and offers plenty of storage. Front - a 10" x 9" side opening zippered compartment, a 12" x 16" zippered compartment with 2 sleeves for cell phone, battery bank etc, 2 pen holding sleeves, plus a 10" x 4" zippered mesh compartment.

Straps - thickly padded, mesh lined, and ergonomically curved, with a sunglasses loop on one side. The adjustment hardware is heavy duty plastic that functions smoothly and all of the stress points are well reinforced.

Unit ceased communicating with the base unit in November 2021.

Had Energizer Lithium AA cells installed. Changed out to new AA alkaline cells. No communication with base unit.

Changed "A-B-C" channel from "C" to "A". Still no communication.

The unit has no capability of wifi to my phone.

Display is very very bright. Lights up the whole kitchen/living room. May be too bright for some, though there are three levels of brightness.

I think my next weather station will have a predominantly dark display instead of this predominantly bright display. The new device will also connect to my phone.

To its credit, it has operated in impossibly high Arizona desert temperatures where it read 121 degrees. I'm sure the unit itself was hotter as it was sitting in the blistering sun all day for several years.

Still, being a weather station, one would assume it's *designed* to sit out in all manner of weather, no matter how hot or cold.

text_fidelity_a:
Fire HD 10 Tablet with Alexa Hands-Free, 10.1" 1080p Full HD Display, 32 GB, Marine Blue (Previous Generation - 7th) The Fire HD 10 tablet is pretty much an unbeatable deal for a tablet these days. You get a really good display and decent processor and memory for a great price---especially when it's on sale. And the Fire OS (a rebranded and modified version of Android) works smoothly.

A trade-off is a not-so-good camera resolution.

And there are some limitations on what you can do. If you already own some Android apps, you might not find them in the Amazon app store, and those you do will not credited as paid for. You'll have to buy them again (if you choose to buy).

One option is to follow online instructions for installing the Google Play Store on your Fire. But that's kind of iffy. You don't know when the next Fire OS update might break that installation. And Play Store might download updates to some of the core Fire OS apps that might conflict with proprietary Fire OS modifications.

Another consideration is that this device serves as an advertising and sales platform for Amazon. It's tailored for that. Something to keep in mind.

The thing to consider is if you can be happy with what Amazon gives you. If you're going to be trying to root and work around the OS and app store limitations soon after you get it, maybe it's worth just getting an Android tablet and foregoing the Fire.

If you can be happy with all that, overall it's a great deal for a capable tablet.
text_fidelity_b: Fire HD 10 Tablet with Alexa Hands-Free, 10.1" 1080p Full HD Display, 32 GB, Marine Blue (Previous Generation - 7th)

text_fidelity_a:
Arlo - Wireless Home Security Camera System with Motion Detection | Night vision, Indoor/Outdoor, HD Video, Wall Mount | Cloud Storage Included | 6 camera kit - Eco Packaging (VMS3630B) This is a truly wireless security camera system. The cameras operate on four CR123 batteries each, and lithium-ion batteries are included. That's a big plus, because you can install the cameras most anywhere. Setup took me a little over an hour.

It might be costly to replace lithium-ion batteries regularly, so you might consider getting rechargeable batteries.

The cameras are not pan-tilt-zoom cams. They're fixed. But the mounts are little metal domes, so you can manually aim the camera most any way you choose. The cameras have strong magnets in them to stick them firmly to the mounts. You can also stick the cameras to any steel or iron surface. You might keep in mind that since they're only held by magnets, the cams could be stolen easily if located in easy reach.

You start setup by downloading and installing the Arlo app on your device (phone, tablet, etc.) Then you create an account, agree to the terms, and follow the on-screen instructions for setup. The free version of the app supports up to six cameras.

The Netgear Arlo camera receiver/router connects to your Internet router with an Ethernet cable. It has a wall power supply with a six-foot cord. After it establishes a connection with the Internet router, you then pair the cameras, one by one, with the camera router. That takes about twenty seconds each.

This is where annoying things started. The app has motion detection on by default. Six cameras started slamming my email inbox and notification banner with motion detection alerts. It took a while to find the switch to turn motion detection off. You get to it by clicking on "mode" at the top, then the name you gave your camera system, then click on "disarm."

There's no batch delete feature in the app (not one I could find anyway) to delete all those motion detection videos at once. I had to go through and delete them one by one.

Notifications said the base unit and all the cams needed firmware updates. The update for the base unit went smoothly. The camera updates did not go so smoothly. Almost all of them said "update failed - camera rejected upgrade request." I moved the cameras close to the base unit and retried the updates, one camera at a time. Success.

These cameras do not continually take pictures, which is probably a battery saving feature. They start taking video or pictures only when motion detection is triggered, or when you manually click on "live" on each camera's thumbnail picture. The live stream takes several seconds to start. So the best setting for security would be motion detection active, but that might mean a lot of notifications. If you want to just take a look at the cameras to see what's up currently, that's kind of a problem. Each camera has to be started, and there's several seconds of wait time. (Edited to add: Adding to the wait time is that it appears video clips are not stored locally but rather uploaded to the manufacturer's site then downloaded back to your device.)

Let me put it this way: If motion detection is switched off and you hear the sound of a varmint on your porch and you want to take a quick look or grab a quick snapshot with one of these cameras, that's just not going to happen. You have to rely on motion detection being on to take the pictures for you. With motion detection off, at best you'll be able to take a look after several seconds of camera startup and buffering. (Edited to add: And if the varmint is moving quickly, you may not get a picture of it at all---just the motion detection alert and a short video that didn't capture what set the alert off.)

In contrast, I have three IP cameras that are always on. I can open the app for them and see a live picture from all three cams at once and grab a snapshot from any of them. But they all require hard-wired power, so it's a trade-off.

When you start the app, you see thumbnails from the last time you ran the live streams, or from the last motion detection. Those thumbnails can be hours old. I don't know if it would be possible, but if the Arlo app and cams had a "refresh all thumbnails" feature, that would be a big help in getting a current look at all your cameras. Then you could start live streams if you choose to.

For some reason the app will only support running five live streams out of the six cameras. You have to stop one of the streams to start the sixth.

If you install the Arlo app on more than one device, only one can be logged in and viewing cams at a time.

(Edited to add: A couple of other issues with the app: If you haven't opened the app in a while, you may get a notice that your login token has expired and you have to re-enter your password. More seconds lost if you got a motion detect alert and want to take a quick look. And sometimes you have to dismiss an ad before you can go look at the cams. And on my Kindle Fire, the Arlo app tends to go into some sort of loop sometimes, and I have to shut down and reboot the device.)

Picture quality is good. It can be set to lower resolution to maximize battery life, or medium or high resolution. The cams also have a night vision mode that can be switched off individually using the app. This is handy if you want to position the camera to look out a window at night. If the night vision mode is on, the IR led will reflect off the window at night like a bright light. Turning off night vision mode will avoid that. However, this still requires the exterior to be well lit or to have an outdoor IR source. The cameras' built in IR illumination isn't long range. It will light an average size room though.

The manufacturer says the cameras are weatherproof and can be positioned outdoors.

The web site says the cameras have a 300-foot range line-of-sight. One camera I placed about fifty feet from the router had difficulty connecting. It seems that the number of walls and other items between the camera and the router can have a big effect on connection, which isn't unusual with any wireless devices.

I think for a basic security system, IP cameras might have a few advantages over this system. But this system has its points, such as install-anywhere convenience and fairly simple setup. For actual security, keeping the system motion-detection armed and just letting the cameras grab and upload pictures and the app send notifications is the best solution, I would think. If you want to monitor live pictures yourself, or even just glance at very current pictures from time to time, I'd think this system wouldn't be a workable solution.
text_fidelity_b: Arlo - Wireless Home Security Camera System with Motion Detection | Night vision, Indoor/Outdoor, HD Video, Wall Mount | Cloud Storage Included | 6 camera kit - Eco Packaging (VMS3630B)

text_fidelity_a:
Linksys WiFi Extender, WiFi 6 Range Booster, Dual-Band Booster, Internet Repeater, 2,000 Sq. ft Coverage, Speeds up to (AX1800) 1.8Gbps - RE7310 You should know up front that this extender only works wirelessly with dual-band WiFi routers (routers with both 2.4GHz and 5GHz).

But it will work as a hard-wired range extender for single-band routers (2.4GHz) using an ethernet cable.

If you have a single band router like we do, it will not detect the wireless network or connect wirelessly. If our neighborhood is any indication, this extender won't work with most home routers. Out of the ten or so visible wireless networks in our area, the extender only detected one or two. The two it detected were two of the weaker signals, but I assume were dual band signals the extender would work with.

After several frustrating attempts to get it connected wirelessly, I spent about an hour with customer support before being informed of this limitation on the extender. The product listing says "compatible with all Wi-Fi routers," and it may be compatible with all routers if set up as a wired extender, but apparently it isn't compatible with all as a wirelessly connected extender. If you want wireless connection to your router, check your router's capability and make sure it is a dual-band router before ordering.

As I mentioned, I did get it set up as a wire-connected extender using an ethernet cable. And it works well for that. It puts a good strong WiFi signal all over our house and much of the yard. I'm giving it four stars for that.
text_fidelity_b: Linksys WiFi Extender, WiFi 6 Range Booster, Dual-Band Booster, Internet Repeater, 2,000 Sq. ft Coverage, Speeds up to (AX1800) 1.8Gbps - RE7310

text_fidelity_a:
Bluetooth Headphones Wireless Earbuds Sports Over-Ear Bluetooth 5.3 Ear Buds with Earhooks 120H Playtime Wireless Headphones for Workout Waterproof Audifonos Bluetooth inalambricos LED Power Display I find that the best price to performance is in the $30 range for Bluetooth headphones, and they keep getting better and better. I have several pairs that I use for the gym, general listening to music, watching movies, and playing poker. I like to have other charged ones ready to go if a pair gets low.

These were rated very well, so I decided to give them a shot. They are super comfortable and they stay in place at the gym. I am not an audiophile, but these are well balanced and have better sound quality than my other pairs.

The greatest thing about these is the battery life- I used them for about 11 hours, and there was still 50% battery life left. With all my other pairs the battery life is a real problem, and it does not improve as they age. The charging case is also nice and there is a display for remaining battery life of the case. Remaining battery life of the headphones is displayed on the mobile device.

The BT connection is also super reliable. I have not experienced any disconnects or interference.

There are a couple cons (no product is perfect) and I want to briefly discuss them.

1. The rubber snap-on ear buds are not universal. They have a unique oval shape where they snap on and are secured. I have a bunch of spares, but they will not fit on here. If you lose one or it breaks it is useless. It comes with 3 sizes, but most people are probably like me and can only use the one size that fits.

2. The gain is too high on these. Adjusting the volume from zero, there are not many steps until the volume is too high. This means that micro-adjustment of the volume is not possible. All my other pairs I can use at 100% volume or near this (though I would not recommend it) and there there are maybe 15 or more micro-adjustments all the way back down to zero. Also, the notifications "power on," "power off," and "connected" are too loud. It's possible that with different mobile phones they behave differently, and there may also be an adjustment for this.

In summary, I highly recommend these. They are comfortable, they stay in place, they stay connected to my device, and they sound great. Probably the biggest Pro is the battery life. I purchased these to use as a backup for my other pairs, but it turns out that these will be my main headphones.

text_fidelity_a:
Fire Tablet with Alexa, 7" Display, 16 GB, Blue - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th) I received a Kindle as a gift, and it has taken over my reading life. I'm sad when a book is only available in print and delighted when there is a Kindle version. It's not AS comfortable as a print book, it's MORE comfortable than a print book. The font is amazing. It's easy to use, and for people who knit, it sits nicely in a bookstand on or a reader's pillow to read while knitting.

I have the Sony eReader. I used to own the rocket. I see the Kindle as the real future of ebooks, and I really want ebooks to succeed for a few reasons.

One is storage. If you are a bibliophile, you probably have a book army ready to take over your home. We avid readers are forced to cull our libraries to make room for new books. No more. I would suggest opening a free account with a service like Goodreads to categorize books, since with the Kindle you can't set up a "history" section and a "fantasy" section, but that's so minor. I never could keep those organized in my print library as well, and many books fall into multiple categories anyway. Do I need to mention that ebooks don't yellow and decay over time?

Two is portability. If you are the type to carry many books at once (I am--some for study and some for pleasure reading along with a newspaper) then this is the easiest way to do it.

Three is the glorious possibility that books will never go "out of print" again, because there is no "print" overhead, just a little meg sitting in a several terrabyte raid array somewhere. Books will always be a minute away.

Four is the idea that books will be instantly large print and still small, and easy to tote around. My eyes are still quite good, but I'd love to think, when age degrades them someday, I'll still be able to read the latest releases easily.

Five is the instant availability of hot books. When Brisingr came out, it was sitting on my Kindle that morning. Compare that to the sometimes day-long wait we went through for the Harry Potter books (and books that size are yet another reason ebooks rock). I love having the New York Times delivered, but can't stand it when the delivery boy loses the key and rings my bell at 4 in the morning. This is the best of both worlds.

Six is the ease of reading large online documents, such as those from Gutenberg or a friend's novel (and don't we all have someone who sends us large files to read from time to time?)

Seven is the price of the books. Everything is cheaper on the Kindle and some books are frighteningly inexpensive. I bought the Talmud for 99 cents. A collection of the first five books in the John Carter on Mars series for 99 cents. And the entire collection of the Wizard of Oz books for, you guessed it, 99 cents.

Other e-readers hit close to the mark; the Kindle got it right. I only want two things. I want color and I want Amazon to hit that goal of having every book (including comics and manga please) available for the Kindle. Overall, the day of the ebook truly arrived with the Kindle and I couldn't be happier.
text_fidelity_b: Fire Tablet with Alexa, 7" Display, 16 GB, Blue - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th)

text_fidelity_a:
NETGEAR Nighthawk 4-Stream AX4 Wi-fi 6 Router (RAX40) – AX3000 Wireless Speed (Up to 3 Gbps) | 1,500 Sq Ft Coverage Bought this router a few days ago and have already begun the return process. I didn't have a good gut feeling about this router from the start, partly because the reviews are not all raves and partly simply because it looks kind of...evil to me. I am definitely not a fan of the hyper-aggressive router design trend that seems to be targeted at adolescent male gamers. I do not look at this thing and think it looks cool and feel positive feelings; I look at it and feel...apprehension. As a physical object, it's not something I really want in my apartment. But I decided to give it a try anyway because I don't think that kind of gut feeling should be one's primary consideration in choosing a router, and because I often like having the latest, cutting-edge tech and thought it would be nice to be ready for Wifi 6 for when I eventually get an iPhone 11 or some other device that features that protocol. But unfortunately, the negative experiences do not come only when I look at the thing.

I was at first alarmed, as I set up the router, by what a very long time it took anything to happen in the app. At every point at which I so much as switched to a different screen in the app, both during and after setup, the app would chug for an alarmingly long time before finally displaying the page I'd navigated to. This is to be expected when the router needs to restart, but...these were not points at which the router needed to restart. These were not points at which I'd changed any setting at all. These were points at which nothing at all had happened except that I'd attempted to go from, say, the app's main page to the Device Manager page, or the Wifi Settings page, or wherever. Simply switching pages in the app would take 20 or 30 seconds or longer. Another negative first impression.

I also noticed that the app doesn't give me access to a lot of the features of the router I expect to have access to. Granted, I'm an advanced user compared to a lot of people - networking is an aspect of computing I've enjoyed mucking around in for decades now, and my inclination with a new router (or an old one, for that matter) is to dive straight into areas of the settings where many ordinary users may fear to tread. But the Nighthawk phone app appears to be targeted more toward the average consumer. Which, if you're more the average consumer, is fine. But if you're me, you find that to be a disappointing restriction.

Then I started trying to use the web UI instead, and while it gave me access to all those more techy parameters I sought, I found the same delay problem happening when I tried to switch from one page of settings to another, but here it happened for longer, and sometimes the target page wouldn't load at all until I clicked again, this time on the blank page with the spinning progress indicator in the center.

So both of the means I have for interfacing with the router are inordinately slow, and one of them is clunky and glitchy on top of it.

And finally, add to all this the way I will occasionally go to navigate to any ordinary webpage and be told my browser can't display the page because I'M NOT CONNECTED TO THE INTERNET, and voila! - the straw that broke the proverbial camel's back.

This happens, and I go and look at the router to see if maybe it's restarted itself for some reason (automatic software update?) and...no. All lights are on and looking as they do during normal operation; the router's just not providing said normal operation.

I never once had such problems with the Apple AirPort Extreme I replaced with this router, nor with the Linksys AC5400 I bought more recently and then wound up giving to a friend. So, because I want a router that, unlike the AirPort Extreme, is tri-band, is still supported with software/firmware updates, and might also feature better performance with multiple connected devices, I bought myself another AC5400 with which I will be replacing this unsatisfactory Netgear thing as soon as it arrives.

And also because I decided I can wait for Wifi 6 until such time as I actually do have devices capable of taking advantage of it, which may be quite some time (i just bought a new MacBook Pro which doesn't support it, and I don't see the iPhone 11 as having any compelling advantages over my iPhone XS Max, soooo...).

The Linksys AC5400 is a monster among 802.11ac routers and has garnered much respect in tech mags and blogs and so forth. Plus I myself have about a year's experience with one and it's been fast, reliable, and glitch-free. So if you're looking for a new router and don't feel compelled to buy into 802.11ax just yet (few devices support it yet anyways), I heartily recommend that one.
text_fidelity_b: NETGEAR Nighthawk 4-Stream AX4 Wi-fi 6 Router (RAX40) – AX3000 Wireless Speed (Up to 3 Gbps) | 1,500 Sq Ft Coverage

text_fidelity_a:
Panasonic SC-BTT195 Energy Star 5.1-Channel 1000-Watt Full HD 3D Blu-Ray Home Theater System with Tall Boy Speakers Good sound for the money and does what I expected. Skip to the summation if you are looking for reasons not to purchase.

Might be a better choice especially if you own a Panasonic TV as the set up is designed for a Panasonic product line. I had to use their support call service a few times and as most companies today, some are very good and can understand and help, but most will read a prewritten script and hope they hit on the problem you are experiencing. Cons: Had to go buy after market speaker wires due to the lack of length that comes with the system and splice the wires to place the rear speakers. Also had to buy an audio connector to allow the system to produce TV sound. This really ticked me off and Panasonic should really step up and correct these issues. The system also needs to modernize and add another HDMI connection ( and the cable ...really? ) to allow for a cleaner install. Another con is the system will not produce sound while watching the Internet based VUDU movie channel. Panasonic wanted me to buy another movie and call them to "try" some fixes while the movie played! It does work with my cable provided paid movie service. The system would also not work with my top of the line wireless router and had to buy a cable and run wires to their system. One must also buy another adapter ( Dingle) to receive wireless signals that may or may not work or a connecting cable. Check to see see the distance from your router to the system and if it is physically possible to fish the wire to the sound system from the router before you buy the cable.

Summation: "You get what you pay for". If you can splice wires and figure out how to add cables to make TV audio work and the internet work then it's ok. You will need to spend more money on items that should be included from Panasonic and it is best to own a newer Panasonic TV for easier installation. Panasonic kind of ruined what should be a great experience by cutting corners to save money on wire and connections. Panasonic should provide more installation on information "needs" as part of their product description if they aren't not going to provide long enough speaker wire, HDMI connectors and inputs,or audio cables,or internet Dingle or cable.
text_fidelity_b: Panasonic SC-BTT195 Energy Star 5.1-Channel 1000-Watt Full HD 3D Blu-Ray Home Theater System with Tall Boy Speakers

text_fidelity_a:
Lenovo IdeaCentre 3 Desktop Tower, AMD Athlon Silver 3050U, AMD Radeon Graphics, 4GB DDR4, 256GB SSD, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, HDMI, Windows 10 You may know about the announcement from Lenovo a few weeks ago that going forward the company will be certifying all their ThinkPad and Thinkstation workstations for Linux. This computer is an IdeaCentre, not a ThinkPad or ThinkStation, and it comes preloaded with Windows, but I am a Linux user and I wanted to see if it will run Linux.

First things first: If you're looking for a gaming computer or something to handle graphics-intensive programs, this isn't it. It doesn't have a screaming fast processor, although it is a capable one. The onboard AMD Raven graphics module is pretty capable (I tried it out on a big display), but this model has no expansion slot for a video or audio card or any other such upgrades.

It does have a bay for a big 3.5 inch HDD with SATA connectors. And it comes with a 256GB SSD already installed on the motherboard. It also comes with 4GB RAM (and a second slot to add more), and a wired keyboard and mouse and the power supply. It has four USB 2.0 ports in the back, and two 2.0 and two 3.0 (gen 1) USB ports in the front. Also on the front are a card reader slot, the optical drive, mic and headset connection ports, and the power button. The back also has an HDMI port, VGA-out port, and and ethernet port.

It's about the size of an ITX mini tower form factor box, which is a little larger than a big dictionary. It stands upright, so the footprint is pretty small. And it's lightweight compared to a big desktop box.

I didn't even complete the first boot into Windows before attempting a Linux install. Tapping F2 on boot will get you into a graphical menu for picking your boot device, and F12 will get you into a deeper menu for selecting boot order and into the BIOS.

My favorite distro is Debian, so I thought I'd take a shot at installing it. It was a no-go. It didn't have the drivers for the onboard Atheros wifi card, and apparently a few other things. I actually pulled the wifi card off the motherboard and substituted a dongle and gave it a second try. I got Debian installed, but the machine still froze on boot without ever getting into the desktop environment.

So I tried installing Ubuntu, which, along with Red Hat, was specifically mentioned as now being supported by Lenovo. Success. Installation went smoothly. I was still using the dongle for wifi, so I shut down the machine and reinstalled the inboard card. Again, success. Wifi operated right away.

The couple of minor -- emphasizing minor -- things I don't like is that an inboard white LED glows continually when the power supply is plugged in, and as far as I can tell there's no way to turn it off.

Bottom line here is I think it's a good machine for general use. It's pretty capable, but be aware of its limitations so you won't be disappointed.
text_fidelity_b: Lenovo IdeaCentre 3 Desktop Tower, AMD Athlon Silver 3050U, AMD Radeon Graphics, 4GB DDR4, 256GB SSD, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, HDMI, Windows 10

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech Harmony Ultimate All in One Remote - Discontinued by Manufacturer I've had the Harmony One remote since the day it came out, and now "upgraded" to the Harmony Ultimate Remote.

Build and Setup:
This is a very solid remote. It is heavy for its size with clean lines and elegant design. Inside the box is the powered hub with two remote blasters, remote, base, and power cords for the hub and the base. There does not appear to be a removable battery like with the Harmony One.

Set up was very simple. As I already had my settings in myremotesetup.com, I simply had to log into myharmony.com, transfer my settings to the new remote and the remote was setup. It was very easy.

The difference between this remote and other Harmony remotes is that this has a hub and blaster units that connects through your wireless network to allow you to connect and control your units with your smartphone.

You have to connect the hub and blaster units around the units you want to control. It has to be connected to your home wireless network, which was easy. You can either do it through myharmony.com or by pressing the setup button on the hub and your router (if it supports it) it was that easy.

I have my hub on the shelf with my Blu Ray, Dish Box, and Xbox. The one blaster is near the television, and the other is on another shelf with my Wii and my surround sound box. When you go into advanced settings on your remote you tell the remote to control the devices with either just the remote, with the hub, blaster 1, blaster 2, or all of them. This allows flexibility where you setup and place your devices and blaster and hub units.

Using the Remote:
The remote is easy to use. Many of the major buttons; play, pause, fast forward, volume and such are hard buttons on the remote. The remote has a large touch screen that can do all the other device options you may seem fit to try. It scrolls across several pages: Home screen allows you to choose between actions such as watch tv or dvd, channel favorites (which you program), current action screen that controls actions related to what you are doing, and finally the number screen, here is where you can enter numbers to change channels. This last part is a bit of a pain as when I am channel surfing I like to be able to press number buttons to change channels and you really can't do this with this remote without looking.

To operate DVR like functions you can also swipe up from any screen to access a black screen where you can program gestures. By default you press to pause, swipe right to skip forward, swipe right to swipe back, etc.

Phone App:
The phone app for the android is a bit lacking as it is not quite as sophisticated as the remote itself, but can do most of the actions of the remote as long as you are connected to the same wireless network as your hub is.

Troubleshooting:
The remote is easy to use and troubleshoot, Simply rebooting or re-syncing the remote can resolve most problems I've found. It also prompts you for assistance the first time you add an action or new device.

Overall this is a great remote. This will demand, though, some knowledge on your part as it is a very sophisticated remote. Many problems that occur can easily be resolved by some knowledge of networks, remotes, or Harmony devices in general. If you have experience with this you will enjoy the functions and capacity of this remote.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech Harmony Ultimate All in One Remote - Discontinued by Manufacturer

I will say the cube’s remote is better than my Apple TVs but overall at this point the Apple TV is a much better device. No wonder it cost more.

I probably will not buy another Lenovo after this experience. I hope this review helps someone else who runs into the same problem.
