text_fidelity_a:
NETGEAR 8-Port Ultra60 PoE Multi-Gigabit Ethernet Plus Switch (MS108EUP) - Managed, with 4 x PoE++ and 4 x PoE+ @ 230W, Desktop or Wall Mount, and Limited Lifetime Protection I received this item through the Amazon Vine program, although the usual green writing may not be shown. The review is specifically for model: GS305EPP.

Port Binding: I noticed that the Netgear chart shows for the "plus" series of switches, that only models with 16 or more ports support port binding. However, through the web interface, I was able to do a single instance of port binding (it looks like it allows you to bind up to four ports, although I can't think of an instance where binding more than two ports on a five port switch would be worthwhile). I learned some quirks about port binding in the process, that using 802.3ad with multiple Linux servers doesn't allow for more than a Gb of data in any one direction anyway. BUT this switch does apparently support balance-rr, because I could get almost 2Gb/s over a 2Gb aggregate link. I think my hard drives in those machines were maxed out at that point. As I understand it, balance-rr has a high error rate because it uses striping and not all machines support it. But it was working quite nicely with my NAS units and this switch (I was expecting the 8 port switch, which would have made that setup more worthwhile because I could fatten the links on all three servers.

Although my current Netgear Pro AP does not have two ports for binding, I did have an AP before that supported it, in which case that feature on this switch may be an excellent option (particularly considering it is PoE). I haven't done the math for myself, but I think that port binding is almost a gimmick on APs because there is so much overhead on WiFi that even if your AP has a throughput in the multi-Gb range, enough of that is overhead created by the AP that you're not actually getting that much data from one computer to another.

Insight and Web Interface: The Insight App shows this switch (and my Netgear APs) as having "limited support" (just shows basic device info and a link to the device's webpage), so they're not really trying to get users of the "plus" line to subscribe to that in perpetuity.

And you don't need the app to use the switch. You don't even need the configuration page, really: I just plugged this into my old 24-port unmanaged Netgear workhose and it picked up an IP from the router and worked just like an unmanaged switch until I decided to give it a static IP and manage it.

I was really surprised how many features are packed into the management software, considering these are Netgear's lower line of managed devices. But most of the stuff you'll see on huge enterprise devices is here as well (well, it's been a while since I've been inside the big enterprise stuff, but all those goodies reach us as consumers before long).

The web interface is just like any other network device - you can reach it from any webpage and it is super GUI - probably just a little more than I really want it to be, but it is very intuitive and you can find everything with a few clicks. I say "super GUI" just because it looks fancier than I need it to. And one thing I find a little irritating is that when you expand one box, it collapses another, so you can't look at everything at once. This doesn't really matter, but I'm old school where I just want substance over style and even style that doesn't sacrifice substance still looks like they're trying too hard.

PoE: Clearly, on this 4+1 port switch, all four of your devices can use a full 30w each, so this is non-blocking in PoE+ as well as throughput. At time of writing, the 8 port with the same power budget was actually cheaper, so you might consider that, even if you can't use all the ports at full PoE.

What is great about this, is that besides just being able to add APs and IP cameras to your network (or even lighting, etc.), you can turn them on and off from the web interface. So I can keep my main AP on PoE (and therefore on my telecom closet's backup power supply), and then turn my detached garage's AP on and off from the web interface rather than having to go down to the basement and plug or unplug the PoE injector every time I want to use the garage AP (I just turn it on if I'm going to be working out there and might need to watch some "how-to" videos or control my audio system from the local LAN).

*Netgear, if you're listening, I would love to have a super lightweight (and free) app that works remotely (when not necessarily on LAN) to turn ports on and off for exactly this type of reason.*

Construction: Solid device, very dense and professional looking. Plenty of lights that tell you a lot from a glance. Power supply is external and about as big as the device itself. Would personally love a way to rack mount this AND the power supply (for maximum flexibility) in 1 RU, but of course I realize most people don't want to waste a whole rack unit on 5 ports. But for the space both pieces take up, it's about a mid size unit that could be mounted with "wings". It does have four-way keyhole mounts for wall-mounting.

Background: I have great experience with Netgear for my home (but way better than most homes') network. I'd definitely use all their devices were I doing work for small or medium sized businesses. I like them just a tad less when they start trying to sell you subscriptions (which is what I hate about Brocade and Cisco, along with all the proprietary garbage), but for the most part, Netgear is inexpensive and quite reliable. I've had a 24 port nonblocking unmanaged Gb switch running 24/7 in my dusty basement for over 15 years without a single fault AND they still sell that model. Their APs are the best I've had, and I don't think I've ever had a Netgear item break on me, period. I have had lots of other home/SMB stuff break or otherwise have strange issues, though.

That said, there's a lot of no-name PoE switches on the market right now. I don't need any of those handling my low voltage needs OR my data. And they won't beat this line on the price by too much anyway.

This is an excellent device which adds a lot of versatility to your network.
text_fidelity_b: NETGEAR 8-Port Ultra60 PoE Multi-Gigabit Ethernet Plus Switch (MS108EUP) - Managed, with 4 x PoE++ and 4 x PoE+ @ 230W, Desktop or Wall Mount, and Limited Lifetime Protection

Garmin vívoactive HR GPS Smart Watch, Regular fit - Black My in-depth review of the new Garmin Vivoactive HR that debuted this week ($249/AMZN) and that I've been wearing since Saturday is as follows:
-- It buzzes and vibrates a lot. Not sure what it's doing because by the time I look the message has disappeared.
-- I ran with it and managed to stop it at 1.46 miles and don't know how I did that. Had to restart another run. I should be able to figure this out in about 3-4 months.
-- It is counting my steps for some reason and I really don't care how many steps I take. My goal is to take as few steps as possible to get where I need to go, especially if where I need to go is the bathroom
-- It's waterproof and can be used in the pool for lap swimming, yet I've still taken it off each time when I shower. I don't know why.
-- It has a green light under it that's tracking my HR at all times. When I was running it showed my HR was elevated. This was not suprising in any way, considering I usually look like I'm in the midst of an anuerism when I run, even if it's just to the bathroom.
-- It is "tracking" my sleep. I found the little screen that showed my HR while I was asleep and or/if I was "deep sleeping" or if I had any movement. Unless it can help me remember what I was dreaming about, or at least stop dreaming about being back in High School with no pants, I plan on taking the watch off when I sleep.
-- I was able to sync it to my phone and put the Garmin Connect App on my phone. Both are legitimate milestone events for me. Now whenever I get a text message on my phone my wrist buzzes and my phone beeps. The writing on the phone is small and I can't see it without my glasses, so I don't need this, especially since my phone has to be close by for the bluetooth to even work. This seems redundant and at some point I'll figure out how to stop this.
-- Other things it shows are the weather (again, it's on my phone which is 2 feet away), and "intensity minutes". I don't know what Intensity Minutes are, but I'm wondering if that would include me stressing out looking for my keys each morning or trying to convince my child that she needs a shower.
-- It's impossible to see the screen in the dark. I run in the dark. Now I need to bring a light to see how far I've run in the dark.
-- The app for my phone for Garmin has all sorts of things on it as well, mostly the same things we see on the watch, but with loads more information such as circles, graphs, and lines. It continuously tells me that it's not synching with my watch, but my watch has the little BT symbol showing, so I think it's purposely pi#‪#‎ing‬ me off to add on some Intensity Minutes.
Overall, it's black and tells the time. If I remember to wear it and start it when I run, it'll tell me how long it took to do my runs and how far I went, which was never really that important to me in the first place.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin vívoactive HR GPS Smart Watch, Regular fit - Black

RackPath 1U 19 Inch Plastic Server Rack Mount Cable Management Duct Raceway with Panel Cover For the record, I prefer the European-version of the Rittal Cable Management Panels (CMPs) that are just a metal plate with easy to slide into metal arms. But I've never seen them in the States, however, I have seen some sort of similar, but with plastic arms.

This style is much more common in the States, but trying this has helped me to appreciate it a little bit more. I guess I normally don't like them because in "public" telecom rooms (by public, I mean multiple people working on/in them), these type are always so full and messy that no one ever puts the fronts on correctly. In my private telecom cabinet, of course I keep it looking nice. The front closure can maneuver down or up as if on a hinge and snaps into place well. I see now, how routing through the different "fingers" can work very well if you're being careful and care about looks and quality of routing. I have CatX cables going between the fingers, but have some DACs going to the side and in to accommodate a more generous bend radius.

What really works nicely in my case (although I think, ideally you have a wide enough cabinet with enough CMPs that you don't have to do this) is that I can take the cables through the holes in the back plate, circle and secure them, and then come back in the back plate, which mitigates patch cables that are longer than necessary. I honestly can't remember if the big brands have those holes in the base plate.

In a home situation, I'm not going to have problems with the fingers bending and the cover no longer fitting on because I take care of my stuff.

Oh, worth noting is that this does not seem to be as deep as the ones you see in data centers by the big brands. They may have done that on purpose, figuring a lot of homeowners don't have 100cm deep racks (or, if they do, they didn't allow for enough space in the front).

Overall, this is very good for me. I'm not sure if they're making these for the homeowner/power user market, or trying to break into the data center world, but it certainly works for the former.
text_fidelity_b: RackPath 1U 19 Inch Plastic Server Rack Mount Cable Management Duct Raceway with Panel Cover

Rosewill 3.5 Inch Hard Drive Enclosure to USB 3.0 / eSATA. External Hard Drive Case Aluminum Body, Built-in Cooling Fan and Fan Switch. Support 3.5” SATA III / II / I Hard Drive up to 6TB and UASP function. Wouldn't recognize on the eSATA port. It would detect the HDD, but would not format nor store data. I thought it would be plug and play. I submitted a return request (which the seller approved), but after extensive Googling, discovered how to make it work on my machine.

1) For Windows 7 (I think Windows 10 may not have this issue), make sure you have the registry entry to allow AHCI.
2) In BIOS, make sure your boot devices are in proper order.
3) In BIOS, update RAID configuration to AHCI.

After that, it is operating as expected.

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Oasis E-reader with Leather Charging Cover - Black, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi), Wi-Fi + Free Cellular Connectivity, Built-In Audible (Previous Generation - 8th) I've been an avid fan of ebooks since the long gone days of the Rocket and the eBookman, and a fan of the Kindle since the very beginning. This is miles and away the best there has ever been. It is a luxury model, no doubt, but oh is it luxurious.

I like:
The weight. Even in the case it's very light, though if it gets much lighter I'll worry about it blowing away in a strong wind.
The size. It's not going to get much smaller without shrinking the screen.
The interface. I'm sorry, I like buttons. Call me old. I never bent back the spine of a book (horrors) so I can't compare the feel of this to that, but I can say it's nice for a long reading session. The touch screen takes a bit of getting used to, but the tutorial will guide a new user. The tutorial is intrusive at first, but provides useful information and goes away quickly. I will suggest customizing the screen. I hated the default, but you get a lot of options to make it just the way you want.
The lighting is now all but invisible. I was unhappy that you can't completely turn it off as you could with the Nook Glowlight, and turning it down casts an odd yellow light over the page, but it's so even now as to be so unintrusive I barely notice going from sunlight to tunnel on the bus home. With the Nook I'd be thrown out of the book to go turn on the light. With the Kindle, I can keep reading without a pause. It does not have adaptive lighting, but I'm not sure it needs it.
The download speed. I don't know if it's supposed to be faster than the Kindle Keyboard (the last one I had with 3G) but it certainly seems that way.
The battery life. Maybe with this thing going for months we'll finally hear an end to the "but my dead tree doesn't run out of power" nonsense.
Next in series. When you're almost done with a book, it tells you where the story continues. Now the next feature I want, and if it does this I haven't seen it yet, is an alert when the next book in a series I'm following is published. Yes, FictFact is great, but I'm greedy and want it right on the device.

I don't like:
It's not waterproof. There was a lot of hope it would be after the Nook went that route.
It's not solar, yet, but there are rumors of a solar cover coming soon.
It doesn't support Audible and the excellent immersive reading between ebook and audiobook. I have a weird love of that feature, seeing what changed print to audio.
Recommended Content and Reading Lists. I shut this feature off. The information seems scattered at best and gave me no useful information, especially considering how precious screen real estate is.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Oasis E-reader with Leather Charging Cover - Black, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi), Wi-Fi + Free Cellular Connectivity, Built-In Audible (Previous Generation - 8th)

text_fidelity_a:
HP 1KF76AA#ABL OMEN by Wired Gaming Headset 800 (Black/Red) Bear in mind that as gaming headphones, the sound quality is not as suited for other applications like listening to music. Having said that, here's how the experience went:

Appearance: maybe this is some macho thing, but they are enormous and intense-looking in an almost exaggerated way. So if you're one of those people that likes huge flashy stuff or ostentatiously masculine-looking things, this is perfect? They're huge.

Comfort: Very comfy! The cup part is large and fits great, and the headband adjusts nicely to most average head sizes. The microphone is fully adjustable, making it work for anyone.

Sound blocking: pretty good! While it does not use noise-cancelling technology, the sheer size and generous build of the headphones allows for Very effective sound cancellation. I had my partner listen to something with her back to me so she could not see me, and with the volume turned up, I had to full on Scream for her to hear me.

Sound quality: Better for spoken word and voices, honestly. The sound is crisp and detailed, but it's also a little canned-sounding, with somewhat sharp, tinny trebles and less-than-intense bass. This does best in mid-range and capturing voices and sounds, and less so for actual music. Having said that, it is certainly better than cheap headphones for music, so it does have some versatility if you're not too picky.

Overall: These are pretty great! They even have an adapter that can be used by other devices that unites the audio input and output, which comes split for certain applications like computers or other gaming. (Meaning, theres a separate cable for the microphone and audio input, and they come with an adapter to have a single "female" connection that can work on phones or other single-plug devices using audio in/out.)

Cool!
text_fidelity_b: HP 1KF76AA#ABL OMEN by Wired Gaming Headset 800 (Black/Red)

text_fidelity_a:
TP-LINK TL-PA511 KIT AV500 Powerline Gigabit Adapter Starter Kit, up to 500Mbps I wish I would have tried these a long time ago. Could have saved me a lot of aggravation over the years. I'm sure a lot of people have heard of these and are likely sceptical. At least that's my excuse. That and I live in an old house with old wiring and many circuits. It's a San Francisco Victorian with bent hallways and a nightmare for both cell reception and WiFi range.

I have wanted to get networking from the back of the flat to the front. That seemingly simple concept never works. What I did get to work was to put WiFi in the back, and then a WiFi extender in the front with a 20' antenna extension which then pushed the antenna to the middle. Even that was tricky.

I even once tried a Verizon 4G LTE router to get some broadband in the front. It was expensive and still didn't work. So I pretty much resigned myself to just running cat5e or cat6 cable down the hallway, which is what I wanted to avoid. But right before I did that I decided to give this a shot.

The install took all of 5 seconds, seriously. Plug a box into one outlet in the back of the flat. Plug that box into my switch. Now run to the front of the flat. Plug that box into an outlet. Run the Ethernet from that box to my switch. Plug Linux box into switch. Boot up and test the speed. 53 MB/sec down, 4 up. Pretty much my ISP limit. My only concern is security, but they do have software, but it requires Windows I bet. I use Linux. I'll see what I can do to lock this down. But it does work. Fantastically so. Not sure the front and back are on the same circuit. Guessing they are. Either way, I finally got the front connected to the back without WiFi or a long Ethernet running down my hallway. And that is 5 stars!
text_fidelity_b: TP-LINK TL-PA511 KIT AV500 Powerline Gigabit Adapter Starter Kit, up to 500Mbps

text_fidelity_a:
Sony Xperia Ear Duo True Wireless headset – Black EDIT: Sony sent me a replacement unit under warranty because of the broken charger. The new unit works as advertised, so I'm upgrading my review to 3 stars. Some users may rate this more highly because of your needs. I give it 3 stars because they are difficult to use, uncomfortable to wear, have mediocre battery life, and are very expensive.

I wanted to give these a fair and thorough test, but unfortunately quality seems to be lacking and it died after just 2 days. First, the rubber ear tip on the right side kept falling off every time I took the earpiece out. Maybe I'm clumsy or maybe it is too fragile, but either way this is really annoying. Second, the battery life is terrible. The battery life indicator dropped from 70% to 30% after just 20 minutes of listening to music. Finally, the charger died. One of the little pins that connected the charger device to the earpiece broke off (or never was attached). Without it, I cannot recharge the right earpiece and since this is a non-standard charger, the whole thing is now useless.

Even if the headphones were 100% functional, here are some general thoughts:
1. Sound quality is very good for headphones that allow you to hear your surroundings. I don't have to take the headphones off to talk to someone standing next to me.
2. That is great because getting these things on or off is much more cumbersome than any other headphone I have ever tried.
3. The user manual really wants you to control these things using finger and head gestures. Maybe my memory is poor, but I can never remember all those things. Even when I'm reading the manual and trying to use the gestures, half the time they don't work.
4. This headset is expensive if all you can do is listen to music and phone calls. They are heavily advertising the "personal assistant" feature as well. The personal assistant feature asks for all kinds of permissions so it can read your messages and emails to you. After the recent Facebook hack, I am really reluctant to grant all these permissions.
5. The personal assistant works best if you have the headphones on all the time instead of just occasionally when you listen to music. However, the advertised battery life of these headphones is only 2-4 hours and my experience is less than that. Constantly recharging these things is a real hassle. Even taking them on and off several times a day is a real hassle.
6. The headphones are cumbersome to take on and off and wear and they are cumbersome entirely because they want to remove the wire between the 2 sides that cheaper headsets have. text_fidelity_a: Beats Studio Wireless Over-Ear Headphone - Matte Black (Old Model) These headphones do have a more balanced sound than the horrible original Beats that were just too bass heavy. The Bluetooth pairing was quick and easy and battery life is decent. The case and accessories seem to be good quality. In all honesty though for the sound quality I'd never pay the retail asking price for these or recommend them to anyone. I got a used pair (yes they are real Beats) for half the price of new and at this price point I feel it's worth it. The noise canceling isn't anything to write home about and if it's a big reason why you're considering these I'd look to Bose or elsewhere where it's done much better. Another point with these is comfort. They're ok for an hour or so, but I'd not want these on pushing two or more. They tend to pinch at the ear cup level and you can see in various pics how the cups nearly touch when not on the head. So the farther you are pushing those cups out the more they are fighting to close so to speak. I don't have a large head, I don't expand the headband at all when wearing, and they get a little clampy after a bit. Another comfort issue is the interior depth of the ear cups. I don't have big ear or ones that stick out and I still feel my ears slightly pushing against the speaker. I couldn't imagine anyone with large ears being happy with these at all and if you fall into that category I'd definitely try on a pair in a store before buying. The cup pads are nice and it's too bad they didn't make them just a tad deeper.  So in summary these are good headphones if not great ones, but honestly not worth retail. The Bluetooth is nice, but you're obviously paying for image here.
text_fidelity_b: Beats Studio Wireless Over-Ear Headphone - Matte Black (Old Model)

text_fidelity_a: Panasonic DMC-ZS40S Digital Camera with 3.0-Inch LCD (Silver) I only have the camera a short time, but so far I am very happy with it. I used a borrowed zs20 on a trip to Peru when my Samsung NX300 died, and loved the panoramic feature and great zoom. The superzoom on this camera is amazing. Just took it to try out on the beach and caught some great shots of birds without scaring them away (see the one legged bird in the attached). Color seems great. I could see taking this as the only camera on a trip. A recent photo enthusiast, so I can't address all of the technical issues, and haven't tried the macro feature etc., so cannot comment on all modes,  but for someone who wants a reasonably small camera with a lot of features, I recommend this one. Has all of the modes available, Aperature and Shutter priority, Auto, Program and Manual, as well as tons of "scene" modes. Range of settings more limited than my other cameras, but this isn't the same type of camera. I am returning the DMC ZS35 I first purchased (20X zoom), because this one has an EVF (hate fighting the washed out display on a sunny day when there is no EVF) and 30X zoom. It was worth the extra money. Purchased used from Amazon warehouse, so happy with the price.

SUDOKEJI 1000W Pure Sine Wave Inverter Power Inverter Peak Power 2000W 12V DC to 110V 120V AC with LED Display 3 AC Outlets & USB Port for RV Truck Boat This worked just fine for powering a few small items. When choosing what you are going to run on this add up the total wattage of all devices, then add at least 50% more to account for peaks or spikes in the power draw. For example if your coffee maker draws 500 watts, your laptop 300 watts, and your toaster 200 watts (total, 1000 watts) you should account for the extra 50% (1000watts + 500 watts (the 50%)=1500watts). In this example, a minimum 1500 watt inverter should be used.

If the item is motor driven, it requires additional start-up (surge) wattage (typically 2-3 times the continuous wattage required) to start the device. For example, a miter saw that runs at 700 watts might require 1400 watts to start up. If your inverter only supplies 1000 watts, you will not be able to start it up. In this case, you would want to select an inverter rated at least 1400 surge watts to handle start-up needs.

I understand how wattage works and for someone who doesn't, any inverter could fail if overloaded with more power than it can handle. An overload feature that automatically shuts the device off would be helpful for anyone who is unsure. This has an overload feature, but if you blow a fuse, you'll have to replace it. Do your research and know how this works, and it'll work fine.
text_fidelity_b: SUDOKEJI 1000W Pure Sine Wave Inverter Power Inverter Peak Power 2000W 12V DC to 110V 120V AC with LED Display 3 AC Outlets & USB Port for RV Truck Boat

text_fidelity_a:
Soundcore by Anker Life Q30 Hybrid Active Noise Cancelling Headphones with Multiple Modes, Hi-Res Sound, Custom EQ via App, 40H Playtime, Comfortable Fit, Bluetooth Headphones, Multipoint Connection These are very good travel headphones. Over-the-ear style is very comfortable when worn for hours at a time. The headphones are relatively lightweight and compact. They fold nicely into the included EVA soft-shell case, which fits easily into my carry-on bag.

The headphones pair easily with my Android smartphone. The Soundcore smartphone app is required for upgrading the headphones' firmware. The app also lets you customize the equalization to one of the presets or you can design your own. Depending on the kind of music you are listening to, the equalizer can make a noticeable difference in clarity and balance.

Unfortunately, the app spams me with notifications about unrelated Anker products. Hopefully this will not be frequent.

Noise cancellation works well. There are 3 modes: on, off (normal), and transparency that lets you talk to people around you without taking the headphones off. Noise cancellation can be toggled both from the app and from a button on the headphones themselves.

Overall, sound quality is good. More of a balanced sound than the boomy default effects that some headphones give. I mostly listen to acoustic music, so this works well for me. Clarity is good. Bluetooth connectivity has been great so far.
text_fidelity_b: Soundcore by Anker Life Q30 Hybrid Active Noise Cancelling Headphones with Multiple Modes, Hi-Res Sound, Custom EQ via App, 40H Playtime, Comfortable Fit, Bluetooth Headphones, Multipoint Connection
